newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya central bank lets market set shilling rate.
newsitem.headline: Kenya central bank lets market set shilling rate.

text.p: Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem said on Monday the bank wants to keep away from intervening on the foreign exchange market, allowing the shilling to find its equilibrium.

Cheserem told Reuters in a telephone interview: "Our policy is changing a bit. What we're telling the dealers is that the (central) bank will not always come in to buy their excess dollars, but that they have to find other avenues."
Cheserem said the bank would enter the market only if it was very volatile or to make purchases of hard currencies for its own needs.
The central bank has previously said a stable exchange rate of 55 versus the dollar was acceptable and five-shilling fluctuations either way were not viewed as being very volatile.
The shilling rallied last week on greater exporters' inflows and dealers said this was possible because of one exceptional factor in the market -- lack of central bank intervention.
The shilling has gained from a CBK commercial mean rate of 54.48 versus the dollar a week ago to 53 on Monday.
CBK chief economist Maurice Kanga said the bank's activity in the market to prevent the shilling from gaining was good for exporters but was too costly in terms of government borrowing.
"We are letting it find its correct levels," Kanga said.
But Joseph Kimura, a finance professor and senior economist at the private Institute of Policy Analysis and Research, said a strong shilling was bad for the economy.

"We are an agricultural country. A strong shilling helps importers and I don't know what importers are doing to help this country's economic growth. Capital inflows in the last three years are very minimal," Kimura told Reuters.
Dealers said they saw the central bank as not intervening in the market last week because of an economic review mission to Kenya by the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
Cheserem rejected the suggestion, saying it had to do with the new policy of letting the shilling to balance itself on supply and demand.

Dealers said the market was slightly nervous, unsure of the shilling's near-term direction. "We're very nervous," said a dealer from a leading commercial bank. "The way things are right now, the market could move 50 cents either way."
A number of dealers said they were trading hesitantly, maintaining wide spreads until they received a clear indication as to the shilling's near direction.
The question on whether the shilling would gain further depended on the extent of central bank's participation in the market. Market analysts said shilling gains were long overdue.
